Okay, page three. What actually is a computer?
A computer is a machine used for storing and processing data by following instructions given to it in a program.
And because you can change the program, the same computer can be a word processor one minute and a game the next.
But a computer doesn't have a brain. It can't think or have its own ideas. It does exactly what its instructions say, just very fast and very accurately.
A network is made when two or more computers are joined together, so they can communicate and share things like printers and files.

Examples: the internet, the biggest network in the world. Your home WiFi, with your phone, laptop, console and smart TV all joined to your router. Gaming networks like PlayStation Network. And social networks like Instagram or TikTok.

Page five: files and folders. A file is one piece of saved work, like an essay, a photo or a song.
A folder is a container that holds files and other folders. Like the ring binders in your schoolbag.
The file extension is the part after the dot at the end of a file name. It tells the computer what type of file it is and which program should open it.

Page six: email. Email stands for electronic mail. It's a message sent from one computer to another over the internet.
You need three things: an email account, email software like Outlook, and internet access from a provider such as BT or Virgin Media.

B C C means blind carbon copy. They get a copy, but they're hidden from the other recipients. Handy for a club newsletter going to a thousand people.

F W, for forward. If Jack had replied to Alex instead, it would show R E.
So reply goes back to the sender, and forward goes on to someone new.
And an attachment is a file sent with an email, like a Word document or photo. A paperclip icon shows there's one attached.
Page eight, and a classic mix-up. The internet and the World Wide Web are not the same thing.
The internet is the hardware: a massive global network of computers linked by cables, even under the sea, plus routers and satellites.
The World Wide Web is the collection of millions of websites stored on the internet. You view it in a web browser, like Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari.
Think of the internet as the roads, and the web as the shops you visit using those roads. Email and gaming use the roads too, but they're not shops.
Search engines like Google or Bing help you find pages. They use algorithms, which are sets of step-by-step rules, to do three tasks.
Crawling: programs called web crawlers, or spiders, follow links to discover websites.
Indexing: each website is analysed and stored in a huge database called an index.
And retrieval: when you search, you get a list of relevant pages, with the most relevant at the top.
But the top result isn't always true. Anyone can publish on the web, so check more than one trustworthy site.
Last page: viruses. A computer virus is a program designed to deliberately damage a computer system or make it unreliable.
Like a cold, it spreads, often hidden in an email attachment, a download or a U S B stick.
A virus can corrupt files so they won't open, delete data, steal personal information like passwords, or slow your computer down until it stops working.
To avoid them: don't open attachments from people you don't know. Install anti-virus software and keep it up to date.
Only download from safe sites, with permission from a parent or guardian. And scan U S B sticks before opening files on them.
